newsitem.title: USA: Clinton warns supporters against overconfidence.
newsitem.headline: Clinton warns supporters against overconfidence.

text.p: President Bill Clinton warned supporters on Sunday night not to be lulled into overconfidence by his big lead over Republican Bob Dole in the polls.
Speaking at a Democratic fund-raising gala that helped raise several million dollars for the party's congressional candidates, Clinton said "the big danger" was a low turnout on Nov. 5.

"What I want to ask all of you to do is to promise yourself that every day between now and election day you will contact somebody to tell them they ought to show up" and vote, Clinton said at the New York event.

Clinton, who was to campaign in Ohio and Michigan on Monday, has ignored Republican efforts to goad him into a fight over his party's alleged acceptance of contributions from rich foreign donors. Aides say the issue shows no sign of flaring into political trouble.
Indeed, after a slight narrowing of the presidential race after last week's debate between Clinton and Dole, all of the polls indicate that Clinton has begun pulling away once again.

Clinton's formidable lead over Dole is suggested by a polling compendium put together by the political publication Hotline. It shows the Democratic president leading his rival by a margin greater than the polling margin of error in 25 states with 307 electoral votes.
That is 37 electoral votes more than the 270 needed to win the presidency.
Dole led by a margin greater than the polling margin of error in only nine states with 44 electoral votes.

Clinton planned to play up one of his education initiatives -- direct government loans for college students, a programme that he says saves money for students and taxpayers -- at a rally in Cleveland's Cuyahoga Community College on Monday.
Dole and the Republicans opposed the programme, which is now in use at 1,600 of the 6,500 colleges and universities in the United States.

Later, Clinton flies to Michigan to participate in a groundbreaking ceremony for Detroit's metropolitan airport. Aides said Clinton's foray into each state was to keep Dole, who is contesting the two battleground states, from gaining a toehold in either.
